strengths: The paper targets a genuine and well-motivated bottleneck in differentiable optimization layers (cost of Hessian/KKT-based implicit differentiation) and proposes a coherent alternative: reformulate the layer as a bilevel problem, reduce the active inequality set to linearized equalities (the 'ghost' problem), and use a finite-difference hypergradient that only needs black-box solves. The construction is clean and the active-set equivalence argument (Theorem 4.5 / Theorem B.1) is reasonable.

The solver-agnostic reformulation (Section 5, Lemma E.1) is a nice practical contribution: replacing the upper-level term f by a frozen linear surrogate c^T y lets the perturbed solve be expressed as a simple linear term, so the layer can sit on top of any black-box convex solver (GUROBI, MOSEK, SCS, qpsolvers) without solver-specific backward code. This is a real usability advantage over CvxpyLayer/QPTH/BPQP.

The empirical evaluation is reasonably broad for the claim: three tasks (synthetic DFL, Sudoku LP, SOCP), comparisons against five baselines (CvxpyLayer, QPTH, LPGD, BPQP, dQP), and both convergence and wall-clock/memory analyses. Figures 3–6 and the ablations in Appendix G.2 (gradient cosine similarity, batch size, solver tolerance, QPTH-GPU) support the claims that convergence is preserved while time and memory scale better.

The paper is honest about its central limitation: Assumption 4.3 (active-set identification) is explicitly flagged as strong, Appendix F gives a concrete counterexample showing why it is needed, and a weaker guarantee without it (Theorem F.2) is provided. Limitations and an impact statement are included, and code is released.
weaknesses: The headline theoretical improvement is conditional on Assumption 4.3 (exact active-set identification), which the authors themselves show is essentially necessary (Appendix F). The claimed O(log(1/ε)) hypergradient cost vs. Kornowski et al.'s O(1/ε) is therefore not an apples-to-apples improvement — it trades an assumption for a rate. The practical validity of active-set identification is never measured in the experiments (no diagnostic of correct/incorrect active-set recovery, no ε-vs-error sweep), so the regime where the theory matters most is untested.

The theoretical contribution is largely incremental: the finite-difference hypergradient oracle and the O(δ^{-1}ε^{-3}) Goldstein-stationary meta-algorithm are directly inherited from Kornowski et al. (2024). The new content is the active-set Lagrangian reduction plus the solver-agnostic linear surrogate. The 'matches best-known rate' framing somewhat oversells what is essentially a combination of an existing meta-algorithm with a modified oracle. The general-convex-constraint extension (Appendix D) additionally assumes an oracle that already returns the correct active set (Assumption D.1.1), which assumes away the hard part.

There are technical/clarity problems in the derivations. Equation 4 in the main text omits the dual term ⟨λ̃, h̃(x,y*)⟩ in the second bracket, whereas the proof (Eq. 18) clearly requires it, so Eq. 4 appears to be a typo that affects reproducibility of the estimator. The notation is tangled (λ* is used both as frozen inequality multipliers inside g̃ and as ghost-constraint duals), and the step 'we used λ̃(x)=0' in Eq. 25 is not justified and looks inconsistent with the ghost KKT system in Eq. 14. The constant C in the O(δ) bound depends on the condition number, which is not discussed.

The bibliography is badly garbled and contains many incorrect/duplicated entries (e.g., the 'Paszke et al.' reference is a duplicate of BPQP; the 'Paulus' entries are corrupted; years for Agrawal/Amos/Kornowski/Arbel/Kwon are inconsistent between in-text citations and the reference list; section numbering for Impact Statement/References is off). This is a significant presentation defect for a main-track submission.

The empirical scale is moderate (d_y up to ~800–1000, 2-layer MLPs, 2048 synthetic samples) and the tasks are standard/small. The strong scalability claims ('sublinear scaling', 'near-constant memory') are inferred from a few dimensions rather than demonstrated at genuinely large scale or on real-world decision-focused pipelines. Gradient-unrolling baselines are not compared (Alt-Diff is dropped for being slow), so the 'first-order' comparison space is incomplete.

strengths: The paper addresses a genuinely important bottleneck: computing hypergradients for differentiable convex optimization layers, where KKT-based implicit differentiation is memory- and time-intensive. The problem framing (bilevel reformulation of differentiable optimization) is clear and well-motivated.

Theorem 4.5 / B.1 (active-set equivalence) is a clean and correct result: freezing the multipliers, folding active inequalities into the objective, and linearizing them as equalities provably preserves the hypergradient at the reference point. The KKT comparison in the proof is valid.

The finite-difference estimator and its error analysis (Lemma C.1) are correct: the adjoint identity (Eq. 27) and the linearized perturbed-KKT system (Eq. 25) are handled properly, giving a genuine O(delta) error bound.

The solver-agnostic reformulation (Section 5, Lemma E.1), replacing the upper-level objective with c^T y where c = detach(grad_y f), is a neat and practically useful trick that lets the same backward pass work with arbitrary black-box solvers.

The empirical study is broad: three task families (synthetic DFL, Sudoku LP, SOCP), wall-clock and memory scaling, plus ablations on batch size, solver tolerance, gradient cosine similarity, and a GPU comparison in the appendix.

The paper is generally honest about its central assumption: Appendix F explicitly discusses why active-set identification is needed, gives a hardness argument (Lemma F.1), and offers a smoothed alternative (Theorem F.2).
weaknesses: The core novelty is incremental. The finite-difference hypergradient framework and the overall meta-algorithm are taken directly from Kornowski et al. (2024), and the active-set/linearization reduction is a standard technique. The contribution is essentially a combination and re-application of known tools to a new domain, which may be insufficient for a top venue.

The headline improvement from O(1/eps) to O(log(1/eps)) hinges on Assumption 4.3 (correct active-set identification). Once the active set is known, inequalities become equalities and the O(log(1/eps)) rate is just the equality-constrained result of prior work. The paper's own Lemma F.1 shows that no continuous estimator can achieve o(1) error without this assumption, so the claimed improvement largely assumes away the difficulty of inequality constraints.

The extension to general convex constraints (Appendix D) relies on an oracle (Assumption D.1.1) that returns eps-accurate primal *and* dual solutions; the authors concede they are 'not aware of any algorithm that achieves linear convergence for the dual solution.' This makes the claimed O(log(1/eps)) guarantee for general convex constraints conditional and weakens the claim of a genuine advance over the linear case.

Overclaiming relative to what is demonstrated. The abstract/intro claim to 'improve the convergence rate' to Õ(delta^{-1} eps^{-3}), yet this only 'matches' the best-known nonsmooth-nonconvex rate, so the end-to-end benefit of the improved oracle cost is not clearly isolated or shown to translate into fewer total oracle calls. The claim of being the 'first' method combining all properties is asserted rather than carefully justified.

Empirical comparisons raise fairness concerns: BPQP is reimplemented by the authors rather than using the official release; LPGD is run at a non-default tolerance (10^-12) after the authors found its default insufficient; all main results are on CPU. The motivating advantage of using GUROBI/MOSEK (which are second-order interior-point solvers) is never actually exercised in the experiments, and the method's 'first-order' framing is somewhat semantic since the backward pass relies on whatever solver is plugged in.

Presentation and reproducibility of the manuscript itself are sloppy: the reference list contains multiple corrupted/duplicated entries (e.g., the 'Paszke et al.' entry is actually the BPQP paper by Pan et al.; 'Paulus, R., and Musil, Amos, and L., and L.'; 'Donoghue' for O'Donoghue; inconsistent years between in-text citations and the bibliography). This makes the artifact harder to build on despite the code release.

strengths: Introduces a genuinely clever 'ghost'/active-set Lagrangian reformulation that reduces general convex-constrained lower-level problems to equality-constrained surrogates, closing the O(1/ε) → O(log(1/ε)) hypergradient gap that Kornowski et al. (2024) explicitly flagged as open for inequality constraints.
The active-set equivalence result (Theorem 4.5) is clean and the proof in Appendix B is straightforward, showing the ghost problem preserves the exact hypergradient at the reference point.

Solver-agnostic design is practically valuable: by replacing f with a detached linear surrogate c^T y (Lemma E.1), the method works with black-box state-of-the-art solvers (GUROBI, MOSEK) without a solver-specific backward pass, which most existing layers cannot do.

Comprehensive empirical study (synthetic DFL, Sudoku LP, SOCP) across convergence, wall-clock, and memory, with ablations on batch size, tolerance, GPU QPTH, and gradient cosine similarity; clear wins in memory and backward time on ill-conditioned/large problems.

The paper handles the strong active-set assumption honestly: Appendix F shows via a concrete 1-D example (Lemma F.1) that no continuous estimator can succeed without it, and provides a smoothed alternative (Theorem F.2) — a useful negative/positive result pair rather than a silent assumption.
Open-source PyTorch library with a drop-in interface matching CvxpyLayer supports reproducibility and adoption.
weaknesses: The core machinery is largely inherited from Kornowski et al. (2024): the finite-difference hypergradient oracle, the O(log(1/ε)) equality-constrained analysis, and the meta-algorithm used for Corollary 4.7. The novel part is the active-set reduction, so the contribution is real but incremental and the paper could delineate new vs. borrowed components more clearly.

There is an unresolved inconsistency in the central complexity claim: Theorem 4.6 states O(log(1/ε)) gradient oracle evaluations, while the corresponding proof (Theorem C.2) states Õ(1). Since the estimator itself only requires two solves, it is unclear where the logarithmic factor originates; this needs to be reconciled, as it is the headline theoretical claim.

Assumption 4.3 (correct active-set identification) is strong, and the method additionally relies on accurate primal-dual lower-level solutions to build the ghost problem; the practical cost/robustness of obtaining reliable active sets and multipliers at scale is not fully evaluated (the gradient-quality check is only cosine similarity, not proximity to the true hypergradient).

The 'matches the best-known rate' framing compares against Zhang et al. (2020) by noting that naively applying their algorithm needs second-order information; this is a somewhat weak comparison — the relevant baselines are other first-order constrained bilevel methods, and it is not shown that Õ(δ⁻¹ε⁻³) is genuinely better than the best prior first-order constrained bilevel complexity.

Baseline fairness: LPGD is reported with a tightened tolerance (10⁻¹²) because its default was 'insufficient,' which improves the paper's relative standing; while the ablation in Appendix G.2 is transparent, this tuning choice materially affects the runtime comparison and warrants more careful treatment.
All experiments run on CPU, justified by a lack of GPU batch solvers; this weakens the practical relevance claim for GPU-heavy ML pipelines, and the QPTH-GPU comparison is relegated to the appendix.

Several load-bearing derivations (solver-agnostic reformulation, general convex-constraint extension under Assumption D.1, hardness example) are pushed to appendices, making it hard to verify the general-convex guarantee from the main text; Assumption D.1's oracle and bounded-inverse assumptions are technical and their restrictiveness is under-discussed.
